extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of art history and literary criticism; painters and poets seeking aesthetic principles for Renaissance-era work
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-aesthetic criteria for assessing (and producing) late 15th–16th century Venetian painting (Giorgione and his school) and French Renaissance poetry (the Pleiad). Emphasises choice of subject, musical/formal unity, pictorial technique, and linguistic/cultural strategy for poetry and translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of subject (subordination to pictorial design)
rubrics_metrics.description: In selection of subject, 'the subordination of mere subject to pictorial design' is essential: choose matter or a phase of subject which 'lends itself most readily and entirely to pictorial form' so that subject is subordinated to the main purpose of a picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subjects that can be fully realised by drawing and colour (painted idylls, genre moments). Examples: small groups amid congruous furniture or landscape, musical or play scenes (the Concert in the Pitti). Avoid subjects that demand an articulated story rather than a pictorially self-contained moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspiration to musical unity of matter and form
rubrics_metrics.description: All pictorial art aspires to the law or condition of music: a perfect identification of matter and form, where colour and design wholly interpret the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a unity analogous to music (matter and form perfectly identified). Choose and treat subjects so that painting attains a music-like coherence rather than merely illustrating narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arresting instantaneous motion and passing expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist should reproduce instantaneous motion with 'resolution, the ease and quickness' and arrest 'the sudden act, the rapid transition of thought, the passing expression'—what Vasari called il fuoco Giorgionesco.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop facility for depicting brief, vivid gestures (e.g., lacing-on of armour, fainting lady, a kiss); value vivacity and immediacy. Anti-pattern: static, overly generalized gestures that fail to capture the particular instant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of the significant instant (dramatic compression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select 'profoundly significant and animated instants, a mere gesture, a look, a smile'—brief concrete moments into which 'all the motives, all the interests and effects of a long history, have condensed themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to present a concentrated, evocative moment that implies past and future. Such 'ideal instants' function as consummate extracts of life and are central to Giorgione's pictorial poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between figures and landscape (modulated unison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a true balance: 'that modulated unison of landscape and persons—of the human image and its accessories—so that, in it, neither personage nor scenery is ever a mere pretext for the other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose scenes so figures and setting mutually support one another; avoid using landscape merely as backdrop or figures as mere accessories. Example: Jacob embraces Rachel among the flocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic motifs: music, play, and water
rubrics_metrics.description: Favoured incidents include music or music-like intervals, play/masques, and the presence of water (wells, marble-rimmed pools, pouring water); these motifs lend themselves to the Giorgionesque mood and pictorial poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these recurring motifs to suggest listening, playfulness, or cooling refreshment—they enhance the sense of 'music-like' life. Examples: music heard across running water; woman pouring water in Fete Champetre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmosphere, colour, and 'Venetian clearness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ a luminous, clarifying air—'the air ... seeming as vivid as the people who breathe it, and literally empyrean'—and a refined handling of colour (gold-thread luminosity) to give paintings an aura of delicate, refined splendour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek clarity of atmosphere, subtle handling of light and colour, and a sense of golden refinement in flesh, cloth, and landscape. Avoid muddy or heavy colouring that destroys the empyrean quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and taste in scenic composition ('park scenery')
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery should be 'park scenery'—economised undulations, grouped trees, rustic buildings treated with elusive refinement—so that the landscape is graceful and supports the pictorial poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose landscape elements with restraint for graceful effect; do not overload with irrelevant topographic detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution and evenness of design/execution as authenticity standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'distinction' of a genuine work (used by critics to attribute Giorgione) is its sustained evenness of perfection 'alike in design, in execution, and in choice of personal type.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging attribution/authenticity, look for consistent excellence across design, technical execution, and selection/depiction of types; works lacking that sustained evenness may be by imitators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical method: 'vraie verite'—value of indirect influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should not stop at strictly ascertained facts; beyond authenticated works consider the 'Giorgionesque' influence, tradition, indirect effects and cultural efficacy—the vraie verite that supplements narrow facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance skepticism about attribution with attention to an artist's broader influence and the school or spirit that the name evokes. Don't reduce value solely to a catalogue of authenticated objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: French taste: nicety and daintiness of execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Old French taste is characterised by 'a certain nicety, a remarkable daintiness of hand, une nettete remarquable d'execution'—a light, aerial delicacy and simple elegance of execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In poetry and decorative arts favour fine, delicate touch, refined gestures, and precise workmanship. This is valued even where greater force or seriousness is sacrificed for manner and elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic form and musicality (structure and metre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ronsard and the Pleiad sought greater 'music' in verse by giving form and structure (e.g., strophe and antistrophe, Pindaric ode) and a 'changefulness and variety of metre' to keep the reader's curiosity and to create a visual aspect that 'carries the eye lightly onwards.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate formal structures and metrical variety to achieve musical effect in poetry; consider typographic/page aspect as part of musical presentation. Anti-pattern: monotonous or shapeless verse lacking formal interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation of the vernacular versus reliance on translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Du Bellay argues for ennobling French by adapting classical models into the native tongue rather than depending on literal translations: languages are shaped by 'choice and men's freewill' and not inherently unequal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical models as inspiration but render ideas into the living vernacular; avoid slavish literalism in translation and the assumption that only dead languages can express certain kinds of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of good translation (effect over formal fidelity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Du Bellay's test: a good translation should reproduce in the reader 'the same affections' as the original; he suggests reading Demosthenes/Homer in Latin and Cicero/Virgil in French to compare effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise the emotional and rhetorical effect in translation rather than word-for-word fidelity. Beware of translations that result in constrained, cold, or ungraceful language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and manner in poetry (courtly refinement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pleiad's poetry is 'poetry not for the people, but for a confined circle'—courtly, erudite, and mannered; style and cultivated manner are central to its value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing for this tradition, prioritise refined manner, learned references, and cultivated elegance; such poetry aims at a select audience and embraces ornament and learnedness rather than broad popular appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about pedantry and ephemeral neologisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive pedantry (obsession with orthography and archaic letters) and faddish coinages or imported Greek words may charm briefly but are often ephemeral and can detract from naturalness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use learned ornament and foreign terms sparingly; favour naturalness and lasting elegance over pedantic novelty. Anti-pattern: overuse of curious or invented words that date the poem.
